newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Kohl wants veto on EU asylum policy.
newsitem.headline: Kohl wants veto on EU asylum policy.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl insisted on Tuesday that individual European Union members should be able to block EU policy decisions on refugees seeking asylum in Europe.

Kohl, speaking in an interview with the Pro Sieben German television channel at the Amsterdam summit of EU leaders, said Germany felt it was a "national duty and a piece of self-preservation" to ensure it had a veto on such decisions.
He said Germany, which only four years ago tightened asylum laws that were among the most liberal in Europe, still took in more refugees than all the rest of the EU states together.

Proposals under discussion at the Amsterdam summit would offer the EU full powers over the bloc's immigration and asylum policies, something that has provoked concern among right-leaning German politicians.
There are also plans to extend to other members an existing agreement under which seven EU states, including Germany, operate a border-free zone.
Kohl said it was not anti-European to insist that future asylum policy should require unanimous approval of all EU states, arguing that Germans could otherwise lose faith in the European ideal.
Over seven million foreigners live in Germany, including many from Turkey, Italy and former Yugoslavia who were invited as "guest workers" during West Germany's post-war economic boom.

Numbers have recently been swelled by some 320,000 refugees from the Bosnian war. Since a 1995 peace agreement, German states have said they can no longer afford to keep them, and last October agreed to deport those who did not return voluntarily.
Germany is particularly sensitive to immigration issues after homes for asylum-seekers were targeted in a spate of racist violence shortly after German unification in 1990.

Only last month, suspected right-wing extremists set fire to a northern German church, scrawling its walls with swastikas and the name of a local priest known to have sheltered a family threatend with deportation to Algeria.
